analysis.one_liner: Overhauls immigration enforcement by ending mandatory detention, banning for-profit detention contracts, narrowing deportations for past crimes, and repealing criminal penalties for unlawful entry.
analysis.headline: The New Way Forward Act was introduced in March 2023 with 33 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a hearing or a vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reshape how the U.S. enforces immigration law. It would end mandatory detention, require a custody decision within 48 hours with a presumption of release, ban contracts with for-profit detention companies, limit deportations based on old criminal records, let immigration judges grant relief despite past convictions, and repeal federal crimes for crossing the border. It would also bar state and local police from most immigration enforcement and allow many people previously deported to apply to return.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants facing detention and deportation, including asylum seekers (who could no longer be mandatorily detained), long-term residents with old criminal records, and people previously deported who could apply to come home. Also families and communities that rely on them, and state and local police forces that would be freed from immigration-enforcement duties.

how_it_helps.text: Ends mandatory detention and requires an initial custody decision within 48 hours, a presumption of release, and the least restrictive conditions necessary.
Bars DHS from contracting with for-profit companies to run immigration detention facilities, phasing such contracts out within three years.
Requires immigration judges to consider a detainee's ability to pay when setting bond and bars fees for alternatives-to-detention programs.
Removes many crime-based grounds of deportation, gives judges discretion to grant relief despite past convictions, and repeals criminal penalties for unlawful entry or reentry.
Lets people who were deported or left under orders since 1996 ask to reopen their cases and return at government expense if they would qualify for relief under the new rules.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit detention companies, which would lose federal detention contracts within three years, and electronic-monitoring providers, whose ankle-bracelet programs would be excluded. The government would take on the cost of running detention facilities directly, transporting returnees, and operating community-based case management.

drawbacks.text: The bill narrows the definition of 'aggravated felony' to crimes carrying at least five years' imprisonment and strikes many crime-based grounds of deportability, which opponents would argue lets people convicted of serious offenses avoid removal.

It repeals criminal penalties for illegal entry and reentry and creates a presumption of release with a government burden of proof to keep someone detained, which critics would say reduces enforcement tools and could increase unlawful entry and failed court appearances.

It applies new definitions retroactively to convictions already entered, and lets people previously deported since 1996 return at government expense to reopen cases, which is a major change opponents would call unfair to those removed under the rules in force at the time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — liberty, family unity, and relief from detention and deportation for immigrants — are large for the people affected and cost taxpayers relatively little, and it would eliminate the private detention contract stream. Its drawbacks are serious: narrowing the "aggravated felony" definition and repealing criminal penalties for unlawful reentry would allow some people with serious convictions to remain, and courts could release people the government considers dangerous; the five-year removal limit could shield long-undetected cases. Those tradeoffs are the reason the bill drew no Republican support and even limited Democratic cosponsorship, and an honest supporter would have to acknowledge them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 29, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee.
It drew 33 cosponsors, all Democrats, none of them committee or party leaders.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit detention companies and the existing enforcement system — nothing changed. Immigrant families hoping for relief got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private detention companies and status quo enforcement

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 33 cosponsors.

for.name: Progressive House cosponsors (including Reps. Casar, Pressley, Ocasio-Cortez, Tlaib, Omar)
for.role: 33 Democratic cosponsors, all in the progressive wing
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; none held chairmanships that could advance the bill.

against.name: House Republican leadership and Judiciary Committee majority
against.role: Majority control of the House and the Judiciary Committee in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee the bill was referred to and never scheduled it for a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were Democrats, mostly from the party's progressive wing, and with Republicans controlling the House Judiciary Committee the bill never moved; no Republican supported it.

industries.note: The bill would ban DHS from contracting with for-profit detention operators and force facilities into government ownership within three years, ending a multibillion-dollar revenue stream. Ordinary immigrants gain liberty at that industry's expense.
The bill bans ankle monitors and electronic surveillance as alternatives to detention and replaces them with community-based case management run by nonprofits or government.
